statements.body: The office contains sixty plants that require regular watering care.
A rotating volunteer crew is responsible for watering the plants.
Plants are currently being killed due to coordination failures: some are watered multiple times in a week while others receive no water at all.
The intended interface is a kiosk display located by the kitchen.
The kiosk must show which plants need water today.
The kiosk must show which volunteer has claimed responsibility for watering each plant.
The solution will be a kiosk-based display rather than a mobile app or email-based coordination tool.
How many volunteers are in the rotating crew and how frequently does the rotation change?
What determines whether a plant needs water on a given day — a fixed schedule, a sensor, or manual judgment?
How does a volunteer claim a plant — via the kiosk itself, a phone, or some other input method?
Who is responsible for setting up and maintaining the plant schedule and the kiosk system?

concerns.coverage: Plants are dying because volunteers over-water some plants and neglect others in the same week; the root cause is lack of visible, real-time coordination among the rotating crew.
Volunteer office staff operate the system; sixty plants are the indirect beneficiaries. Crew size and rotation frequency are not yet stated.
The workflow involves determining which plants need water today, a volunteer claiming one or more plants, and marking them as done — but the claim and completion mechanisms are not yet defined.
The system must track per-plant watering schedules and daily claim status; the source of schedule data and how completion is recorded are unknown.
A physical kiosk by the kitchen must stay running and up to date daily; who owns maintenance and updates is not yet stated.
The solution must be presentable as a kiosk in a specific physical location (by the kitchen); no budget, stack, or timeline constraints have been stated.
No explicit exclusions stated yet; mobile app and email-based coordination appear out of scope based on the kiosk decision, but this has not been confirmed by the user.
Success is not yet defined in observable terms; implicitly, fewer plants dying and no duplicate or missed waterings would be the signal, but no threshold or measurement method has been stated.

candidates.body: What determines whether a plant needs water on a given day — a fixed per-plant schedule, sensor readings, or someone's manual judgment?
candidates.whySelected: This is the engine of the whole system: the kiosk's core promise is showing 'what needs water today,' and everything downstream (data model, who maintains schedules, what the first slice builds) depends on where that signal comes from. It is already an approved unknown, so answering it converts the largest named gap into buildable fact.

candidates.body: How does a volunteer claim a plant and mark it watered — by tapping directly on the kiosk, or through some other input?
candidates.whySelected: The claim/complete interaction is the second half of the coordination loop and is currently undefined; whether the kiosk is touch-interactive or display-only radically changes hardware, cost, and the first slice's scope.

candidates.body: Who will own entering and maintaining the per-plant schedule data and keeping the kiosk running?
candidates.whySelected: An unowned kiosk by the kitchen will go stale within weeks; naming the operator bounds operational scope, but it matters slightly less to the first slice than defining the watering signal itself.

readyAdvice.why: All ten concerns have some coverage, but the two mechanisms at the heart of the workflow — how 'needs water today' is determined and how a volunteer claims and completes a task — remain open unknowns. A first vertical slice cannot be bounded until at least the watering-signal question is answered, and success has no observable threshold yet.
